URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2009.2017406, doi:10.1109/tcsvt.2009.2017406. This article has 74 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not specify an optimal camera count or placement for tracking an articulated robot arm, nor does it provide a universal number guaranteeing full visibility. It emphasizes that occlusion and unknown surface visibility are fundamental problems in stereo reconstruction, and that multiple widely spaced cameras help infer visibility and integrate appearance. For full-body capture, reported systems use substantially different configurations depending on the task: examples in Table I include 4–8 cameras for real-time silhouette reconstruction, 8–25 cameras for model-free capture, and a 51-camera dome for dynamic human-scene reconstruction. These examples suggest that camera number must be selected according to required coverage, baseline, reconstruction method, and scene complexity rather than a single fixed optimum. Wide camera placement around the subject (approximately 360° coverage where possible) reduces occlusions during motion, while dense short-baseline arrangements can improve view interpolation but may cover only a restricted viewing range. For a moving robot arm, cameras should be distributed around the workspace and at different elevations, with overlapping fields of view so that at least two or more cameras observe each important surface as the arm articulates. The excerpt supports using more cameras for robust all-around visibility, but does not establish an exact minimum.

The excerpt does not establish a specific optimal number or geometric placement of cameras for eliminating occlusion during articulated-body motion capture. Its proposed method uses one depth video camera, potentially moving, and reconstructs the surfaces of rigid components over a sequence of frames. Because different parts may be occluded in individual frames, the method accumulates geometric information over time and addresses surface reconstruction despite partial occlusions. This indicates that complete instantaneous visibility from one viewpoint is not required when the subject or camera provides changing viewpoints. In contrast, earlier markerless motion-capture approaches based on visual hulls use multiple synchronized cameras observing the subject from several different directions, mainly to obtain silhouettes and overcome viewpoint limitations; however, the excerpt does not give a camera count, spacing, or placement rule, nor does it claim that those arrangements guarantee full visibility of every part of an articulated robot arm. Therefore, the passage supports a distinction between temporal coverage with a single moving depth camera and simultaneous multi-view coverage with several cameras, but it does not specify how many cameras are needed for full visibility coverage or identify an optimal placement configuration.

For silhouette-based reconstruction, increasing the camera count improves shape accuracy; view-angle coverage stabilizes at approximately 16 cameras, after which adding cameras produces relatively little change in reconstruction error. However, achieving reconstruction error below 50 mm in the reported experiment required at least 42 cameras. For stereo reconstruction, camera placement should balance matching reliability against depth ambiguity. The reported optimum for the adopted area-based stereo method is a 25° baseline. In a planar camera-ring arrangement, this corresponds to roughly 14 cameras; the text states that a non-planar configuration requires 14 cameras or more. These values are not a definitive number for full visibility of an articulated body: occlusion depends on the arm’s range of motion, body geometry, and camera placement. The excerpt emphasizes that surface reconstruction ideally needs every surface region visible in multiple camera views, so cameras should be distributed around the subject rather than concentrated on one side. For robust motion capture under self-occlusion, the cited results suggest using a surrounding ring or 3D arrangement, with at least about 14 cameras for stereo geometry, around 16 for stable angular coverage, and substantially more—potentially 42 or more—when high silhouette accuracy is required.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Sicilian fortified heritage is a rich and widespread system, yet at the same time fragile and exposed to risk conditions determined by the geomorphological complexity of the sites, local slope instability, erosion, difficult accessibility and the progressive decay of masonry structures. Castles, towers and defensive outposts are often located on elevated ground, urban margins, steep slopes, rocky outcrops or coastal fronts, in close relation to the historic landscape and to territorial settings that are now subject to increasing vulnerability. These conditions require rapid, sustainable and replicable documentation procedures, capable of supporting knowledge of the monument and a preliminary assessment of conservation issues. The paper proposes an integrated low-cost protocol for preliminary 3D documentation and for supporting the risk assessment of this valuable heritage. The protocol combines low-cost UAV imagery, non-professional video sequences, critical frame selection, SfM-MVS photogrammetry, data quality control and the production of knowledge-oriented three-dimensional models. Particular attention is given to the reuse of images and videos produced by non-specialist users, a vast, still underexploited visual archive that, if interpreted through explicit procedures of selection and validation, can support the 3D documentation of monuments at different stages of transformation. The experimentation concerns three case studies: Castelluccio di Gela, Castello di Agira and Rocca di Aci Castello. These were selected because they represent three different conditions, allowing the transferability of the workflow and the usefulness of 3D models to be tested for the preliminary reading of structures, decay phenomena and vulnerability conditions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Image-based 3D reconstruction is vital in many applications, such as digital twins, smart cities, machine vision, and autonomous driving. In recent years, it has undergone a paradigm shift, propelled by advancements in both conventional photogrammetry and deep learning. This review provides a comprehensive photogrammetric perspective on both conventional and learning-based techniques, a viewpoint that prioritizes geometric fidelity, robustness, handling of uncertainty, and suitability for real-world applications. We first systematically revisit the fundamentals of traditional pipelines: Structure from Motion (SfM), Multi-View Stereo (MVS), and surface reconstruction. The review then details recent progress in conventional methods, highlighting innovations in scalable and efficient SfM, specialized camera models for MVS, and robust surface reconstruction algorithms. Subsequently, we explore the transformative evolution brought by learning-based techniques, including deep SfM, learning-based MVS, differentiable rendering-based scene representation methods (NeRF, 3DGS), groundbreaking feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (e.g., DUSt3R, VGGT), and surface reconstruction including explicit and implicit methods. Emphasis is placed on evaluating whether learning-based approaches genuinely meet photogrammetric requirements such as metric accuracy and reliability, rather than optimizing solely for visual realism.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Furthermore, we conclude by identifying key challenges and research frontiers including generalization across domains, scalability to high-resolution imagery, real-time performance, and uncertainty quantification. By bridging the gap between classical photogrammetry and data-driven 3D vision, this work aims to guide future research toward robust, accurate, and certifiable 3D reconstruction systems suitable for engineering, industrial, and geospatial applications.</jats:p>

The excerpt does not support a simple 1/sin(theta) scaling over the full angular range. For small-to-moderate convergence angles, increasing the angle generally improves triangulation depth (height) precision: the reported precision improves from angles of several degrees up to roughly 50°. In the simulated analysis, however, height error is U-shaped with respect to convergence angle: it decreases initially, reaches a minimum near 90°, and then increases at wider angles. Matching errors shift the optimum somewhat toward smaller angles and increase the errors overall. Thus, at very small angles—such as below 10–20°—depth error is expected to be relatively large and to improve rapidly as the angle increases, although the excerpt does not give a numerical divergence law or a specific 1/sin(theta) fit. For very wide angles, the excerpt reports declining image correlation and more difficult matching because of greater geometric distortion; consequently, depth error begins increasing rather than continuing to improve. The provided text does not specifically quantify behavior above 120°, so it cannot establish an exact asymptotic form there. It also distinguishes the height-error optimum (about 90°) from the overall positional-error optimum (about 60°).

The excerpt reports that triangulation depth (height) error generally decreases as the convergence angle between two images increases, with the strongest improvement occurring for angles from several degrees to approximately 50 degrees. The observed decrease is described as following a power-function pattern, rather than the excerpt explicitly establishing a simple 1/sin(theta) law. For stereo geometry, the cited propagation equations relate object-space errors to image measurement error, flight height, focal length, baseline, and convergence angle; however, the equation formatting in the excerpt is incomplete, so it does not support a precise confirmation of 1/sin(theta) scaling. At very small convergence angles, particularly below roughly 10–20 degrees, the reported results imply substantially larger depth errors and poorer geometric strength. The study excerpt does not investigate convergence angles above about 50 degrees and therefore provides no evidence about behavior at very wide angles above 120 degrees. It also notes that cross-track image matching errors increase approximately linearly with convergence angle, while along-track errors remain near the sub-pixel level, so increasing angle is not uniformly beneficial for every error component. Any claim about a >120-degree regime would require additional stereo-geometry analysis or another source.

The excerpt establishes that triangulation depth precision depends strongly on the ray-intersection, or convergence, angle. For a rectified stereo pair, depth error follows from the disparity relation: increasing baseline and therefore increasing triangulation angle improves depth precision, while disparity or image-measurement error produces larger depth error at greater scene depth. In multiview reconstruction, additional observations improve the estimate not merely by adding measurements, but by constraining the 3D point through multiple ray intersections; the camera-network geometry couples redundancy and baseline. The excerpt does not explicitly state that the error scales exactly as 1/sin(theta), nor does it provide numerical behavior or thresholds for angles below 10–20 degrees or above 120 degrees. Thus, it supports an inverse relationship between suitable convergence angle and depth uncertainty qualitatively, but not the precise 1/sin(theta) law or claims about very wide-angle degeneracy. It also emphasizes that true multiview triangulation is substantially more accurate than fusing independent two-view depth maps, with a reported advantage of at least one order of magnitude in depth accuracy.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Commande référencée vision de l'organe terminal d'un robot de taille de vigne</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">L'agriculture, secteur mondial essentiel, fait face à des défis majeurs liés à la croissance démographique, à la pénurie de main-d'œuvre et à la nécessité de pratiques durables, dans un contexte de vieillissement des agriculteurs, d'exode rural et de changement climatique. La robotique agricole offre une réponse prometteuse à ces enjeux en automatisant des tâches exigeantes comme la taille de la vigne. Une limite majeure des approches actuelles est l'absence de commande référencée capteurs, entraînant de nombreux échecs de positionnement de l'outil de taille. Cette thèse vise à améliorer la performance des systèmes autonomes en introduisant une commande par retour visuel, permettant d'atteindre précisément les poses de coupe malgré les mouvements de la vigne ou du robot. Compte tenu de la structure complexe des sarments de vigne et du caractère encombré des environnements viticoles, une première étude est menée sur les méthodes classiques d'extraction de descripteurs visuels (SIFT, ORB, D-SIFT, etc.) ainsi que sur la faisabilité de l'ajustement de primitives géométriques (lignes, cylindres, etc.) destinées à être utilisées ultérieurement pour la commande. Les résultats mettent en évidence la difficulté de la tâche lorsqu'on s'appuie sur des méthodes classiques. Une approche nouvelle et générale de la taille de la vigne basée sur la vision est ensuite proposée. Elle combine l'alignement de nuages de points par Iterative Closest Point (ICP) avec un asservissement visuel 3D (Position-Based Visual Servoing, PBVS). Quatre variantes pertinentes de l'ICP sont comparées dans le cadre du PBVS pour des scénarios de taille de la vigne : l'ICP standard, l'ICP de Levenberg-Marquardt, l'ICP point-plan et l'ICP symétrique. Une initialisation dédiée de l'ICP est intégrée afin d'améliorer la vitesse et la précision de l'alignement, ainsi qu'une procédure de génération de nuages de points de référence aux emplacements de taille. Des expériences en conditions réelles sont menées sur un manipulateur Franka Emika équipé d'une caméra stéréoscopique, impliquant trois vignes réelles dans des conditions de laboratoire. De plus, ce système est enrichi par un planificateur de points de passage basé sur des nuages de points, fonctionnant en ligne. À l'aide d'un schéma de commande prédictive non linéaire (Nonlinear Model Predictive Control, NMPC), une séquence de poses 3D est calculée en temps réel. Celle-ci est ensuite suivie par un PBVS à référence glissante, garantissant un déplacement fluide sans arrêt. Un alignement de nuages de points basé sur l'ICP, intégrant une initialisation spécifique, est utilisé pour l'estimation de la pose. Des évaluations qualitatives et quantitatives sont réalisées sur un manipulateur Franka Emika équipé d'une caméra stéréo en configuration eye-in-hand, exécutant des séquences de taille sur trois ceps de vigne de complexité croissante. La robustesse du système est validée face à des perturbations imprévues, incluant des mouvements de la vigne et de la base du robot. Enfin, les avancées récentes en traitement visuel basé sur l'intelligence artificielle sont exploitées afin de surmonter les difficultés liées à l'extraction, à l'appariement et au suivi de caractéristiques visuelles 2D, et de permettre un asservissement visuel 2D (Image-Based Visual Servoing, IBVS). Des méthodes basées sur l'apprentissage profond (Deep Learning, DL) sont utilisées pour l'extraction et l'appariement de caractéristiques. Dans cette optique, un jeu de données dédié est constitué afin d'entraîner des stratégies DL pour l'appariement de caractéristiques et la segmentation des vignes. L'algorithme IBVS est conçu de manière à assurer la convergence malgré l'absence d'informations de profondeur. Les résultats d'expériences en conditions réelles sur des vignes sont présentés, à l'aide d'un manipulateur Franka Emika équipé d'une caméra RGB unique. Ce travail se conclut par une discussion et des perspectives de recherche.</jats:p>

{"answer": "## Camera Placement for Triangulating a Tabletop Robot Arm: Quantitative Guidance from Photogrammetry and Multi-View Vision

### 1. Optimal Convergence (Intersection) Angle for 3D Triangulation

The convergence angle θ—the angle between two camera rays at the target point—is the single most important geometric parameter for triangulation accuracy. Classical photogrammetric analysis and empirical studies converge on an optimum near **90°**, with a broad practical sweet spot of roughly **60–120°**.

**Geometric basis.** In the stereo depth relation, the depth component of the reconstructed point depends on the reciprocal of the sine of the half-convergence angle. Weinshall (1990) showed that reconstructed depth is proportional to a disparity term divided by 2 sin(α), where the total convergence angle is 2α, establishing an explicit reciprocal-sine dependence (pqac-00000051). This means that at very small intersection angles, depth uncertainty diverges approximately as 1/sin(θ/2), while at 90° the geometric contribution to depth error is minimized.

**Empirical confirmation.** Di et al. (2016), analyzing multi-image triangulation of lunar images, found that overall positional error reached its minimum near a convergence angle of approximately **60°**, while height (depth) error reached its minimum near **90°** (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000046). When image-matching errors were included, the optimal turning points shifted toward somewhat smaller angles because larger convergence angles degrade image correlation and matching precision (pqac-00000046). Li et al. (2014), studying rover localization with the ExoMars PanCam, found optimal convergence angles of **99–100°** for 6-landmark configurations, **100–108°** for 9–12 landmarks, and a recommended operational band of **70–90°** (pqac-00000042). Olague and Mohr (2002) found an optimal convergence angle around **45°** in their multi-camera setup, corresponding to an approximately 90° inter-camera separation, with their image-error model showing that target-localization uncertainty rises sharply as the incidence angle approaches 80° due to foreshortening (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Error growth outside the sweet spot.** At angles below ~30°, rays become nearly parallel, the system is poorly conditioned, and depth error increases rapidly—approximately inversely with the sine of the convergence angle (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000052). At very small angles (5–15°), Nesbit and Hugenholtz (2019) observed systematic bowl-shaped deformation, substantially lower precision, and larger offsets from reference data (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Above ~120°, the geometric benefit plateaus while image correspondence degrades due to extreme foreshortening and appearance distortion, causing a net increase in reconstruction error (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000022).

### 2. Nadir + Oblique vs. All-Oblique Camera Networks

Fraser's (1984) seminal simulations of a 27-point target array compared six four-camera imaging configurations under identical conditions (image scale 1:40, σ_image = 2.3 μm, inner-constraints datum). The results are summarized below:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Key findings from this comparison include:

- **Convergent θ = 120°** produced the most isotropic precision, with σ_XY = σ_Z = 0.07 mm and very small precision ranges (Δσ_XY = 0.01 mm, Δσ_Z = 0.03 mm), making it Fraser's recommended design for most 3D measurement tasks (pqac-00000028).
- **Convergent θ = 180°** gave the most homogeneous distribution (Δσ_Z = 0.01 mm), though σ_XY was slightly larger than σ_Z (pqac-00000028).
- **Normal + convergent** (a mixed geometry analogous to the user's proposed nadir-plus-oblique layout) performed nearly as well as the all-convergent networks (q = 0.6, σ_Z reduced to 0.09 mm), demonstrating that adding even two convergent views to a nadir-like configuration substantially improves Z-precision (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028).
- **Pure "normal" (near-parallel axis) networks** showed the largest Z-error and the poorest homogeneity, with σ_Z roughly 1.5–2.5× larger than σ_XY (pqac-00000027).

In UAV photogrammetry, Nesbit and Hugenholtz (2019) confirmed that supplementing nadir images with oblique images at **20–35°** tilt improved accuracy and precision by nearly **50%** relative to nadir-only blocks (pqac-00000018). Combination datasets consistently reduced systematic dome deformation, generated more tie points, and produced lower standard deviations than either nadir-only or single-oblique datasets (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015). The precision-to-viewing-distance ratio improved from approximately 1:1000 for nadir-only to about 1:1500 for combination datasets (pqac-00000015).

**Implication for the proposed setup.** A one-overhead plus two-oblique arrangement is a variant of the "normal + convergent" geometry that Fraser showed performs well (q = 0.6). However, the overhead camera provides good XY but poor Z resolution for table-plane-parallel targets. The two oblique cameras provide the convergent rays needed for Z. For near-isotropic 3D accuracy, the three-camera all-oblique alternative (cameras at ~30–45° elevation, spread ~120° in azimuth) would produce more uniform error ellipsoids, consistent with Fraser's finding that the convergent θ = 120° network was the best general-purpose design (pqac-00000028).

### 3. Depth Error as a Function of Baseline, Distance, and Pixel Resolution

The fundamental relationship for stereo triangulation depth uncertainty is well established across the literature. For a rectified stereo pair with baseline B, focal length f (in pixels f_px = f_phys/p, where p is pixel pitch), and target at depth Z, depth is given by Z = f_px · B / d, where d is disparity in pixels. Propagating a disparity measurement error σ_d (typically ~0.5–1.0 pixels for sub-pixel matching) yields:

**σ_Z ≈ Z² · σ_d / (f_px · B)**

Equivalently, in terms of the physical focal length f_phys and pixel pitch p:

**σ_Z ≈ Z² · p · σ_d / (f_phys · B)**

This relationship was derived and confirmed by multiple sources (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010). The key dependencies are:
- Depth error grows **quadratically** with camera-to-target distance Z.
- Depth error decreases **linearly** with baseline B.
- Depth error decreases **linearly** with focal length in pixels f_px (equivalently, with physical focal length f_phys for fixed pixel pitch).
- Larger pixels (larger p) increase depth error for a given physical focal length (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

Lin et al. (2021) confirmed these relationships through a geometric pixel-quantization cone model, showing that increasing baseline or focal length narrows the uncertainty volume, while increasing pixel size or target distance enlarges it (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Llorca et al. (2010) additionally noted that larger baseline and focal length increase the disparity search space and the near-field blind zone, creating design tradeoffs in practical systems (pqac-00000005).

**Numerical example for the proposed setup.** With the Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide (f ≈ 2.75 mm, sensor 6.45 × 3.63 mm, 4608 × 2592 pixels → pixel pitch p ≈ 1.4 μm, f_px ≈ 1964 pixels), a baseline of ~1.0 m, and a maximum gripper distance of ~1.5 m from the closer cameras: σ_Z ≈ (1.5)² × 1 / (1964 × 1.0) ≈ 1.1 mm per pixel of disparity error. With sub-pixel matching (σ_d ≈ 0.3 px), this yields σ_Z ≈ 0.3 mm, which is within the few-mm drift detection requirement.

### 4. Self-Occlusion by the Arm and Camera Count/Spread

Self-occlusion by the robot arm's own links is the primary driver for requiring multiple cameras at different viewpoints. The literature on multi-camera motion capture provides quantitative guidance:

**Angular baseline.** Starck et al. (2009), in their comprehensive study of multi-camera 3D production studios, found that an angular baseline of approximately **25°** between neighboring camera views was optimal for stereo matching, balancing correspondence reliability against depth ambiguity. In a planar ring, this corresponds to roughly 14 cameras for 360° coverage (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038).

**Minimum cameras for stable coverage.** For full-body surface reconstruction, angular-coverage stability was reached at approximately **16 cameras**, after which additional cameras produced diminishing returns in visibility improvement. However, achieving reconstruction error below 50 mm in their experiments required at least 42 cameras (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). These numbers apply to complete surface reconstruction of a complex human body and represent an upper bound for the simpler problem of tracking discrete gripper fingertip markers.

**Non-planar arrangement is critical.** Cameras should not all be placed in a single plane, as this creates systematic blind spots (pqac-00000033). Including cameras at different elevations—including overhead views—reduces phantom volumes from self-occlusion, particularly for an articulated arm that can fold back on itself (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

**Active viewpoint selection.** Kiciroglu et al. (2020) demonstrated that optimizing camera viewpoints based on predicted pose uncertainty can substantially improve 3D pose estimation accuracy, suggesting that cameras should be positioned where they provide the most information given expected arm configurations, rather than in a generic symmetric arrangement (pqac-00000039).

**Practical guidance for a tabletop arm.** For the specific task of triangulating discrete fingertip features (not full surface reconstruction), the occlusion problem is substantially simpler than full-body capture. Fraser (1984) recommended a minimum of **three intersecting rays** (not in the same epipolar plane) at every target point (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). With the arm's ~0.63 m reach on a 1.29 × 1.36 m table, the arm subtends a relatively small solid angle, meaning three well-placed cameras with the wide 102° × 67° field of view should maintain at least two-camera visibility of the fingertips throughout most of the workspace. A fourth camera would provide redundancy for configurations where one camera's view is blocked by the arm's body or by the gripper approaching the camera.

Luhmann (2010) reported that multi-camera photogrammetric probing systems using 2–4 digital video cameras achieve typical accuracy of 0.1 mm over distances of 2–5 m, with the imaging rays intersecting at large convergence angles to yield homogeneous accuracy in X, Y, and Z (pqac-00000032). This supports the feasibility of achieving sub-millimeter accuracy with a small number of strategically placed cameras.

### Summary of Key Quantitative Rules of Thumb

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Recommendations for the Proposed Setup

Based on the literature, the proposed three-camera arrangement (one overhead at 1.2 m, one front-oblique at ~0.42 m height tilted 19° down, one low side camera) provides a reasonable "normal + convergent" geometry. However, several improvements are suggested:

1. **Increase convergence angles.** The front camera at 19° tilt produces a very shallow convergence angle with the overhead camera (~71° from vertical vs. 0° overhead = only ~19° convergence). Raising its tilt or elevation would improve the ray-intersection geometry toward the 60–90° optimal range (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028).

2. **Spread cameras in azimuth.** The literature strongly favors cameras distributed ~120° apart in azimuth rather than clustered on one side, to produce isotropic XY precision and maintain visibility during arm self-occlusion (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033).

3. **Consider a fourth camera.** Fraser showed that going from 3 to 4 cameras improves precision by ~20% under the √m rule (pqac-00000029). More importantly, a fourth camera provides critical redundancy when one view is occluded by the arm.

4. **Elevate all cameras to ~30–45°.** An all-oblique arrangement with three cameras at 30–45° elevation and 120° azimuth spacing would approach Fraser's θ = 120° convergent network, which gave the most isotropic and homogeneous precision (pqac-00000028). This configuration also provides better workspace-clearance views than a single nadir camera."}

### 1. Optimal Convergence (Intersection) Angle for 3D Triangulation

The convergence angle θ—the angle between two camera rays at the target point—is the single most important geometric parameter for triangulation accuracy. Classical photogrammetric analysis and empirical studies converge on an optimum near **90°**, with a broad practical sweet spot of roughly **60–120°**.

**Geometric basis.** In the stereo depth relation, the depth component of the reconstructed point depends on the reciprocal of the sine of the half-convergence angle. Weinshall (1990) showed that reconstructed depth is proportional to a disparity term divided by 2 sin(α), where the total convergence angle is 2α, establishing an explicit reciprocal-sine dependence (pqac-00000051). This means that at very small intersection angles, depth uncertainty diverges approximately as 1/sin(θ/2), while at 90° the geometric contribution to depth error is minimized.

**Empirical confirmation.** Di et al. (2016), analyzing multi-image triangulation of lunar images, found that overall positional error reached its minimum near a convergence angle of approximately **60°**, while height (depth) error reached its minimum near **90°** (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000046). When image-matching errors were included, the optimal turning points shifted toward somewhat smaller angles because larger convergence angles degrade image correlation and matching precision (pqac-00000046). Li et al. (2014), studying rover localization with the ExoMars PanCam, found optimal convergence angles of **99–100°** for 6-landmark configurations, **100–108°** for 9–12 landmarks, and a recommended operational band of **70–90°** (pqac-00000042). Olague and Mohr (2002) found an optimal convergence angle around **45°** in their multi-camera setup, corresponding to an approximately 90° inter-camera separation, with their image-error model showing that target-localization uncertainty rises sharply as the incidence angle approaches 80° due to foreshortening (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Error growth outside the sweet spot.** At angles below ~30°, rays become nearly parallel, the system is poorly conditioned, and depth error increases rapidly—approximately inversely with the sine of the convergence angle (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000052). At very small angles (5–15°), Nesbit and Hugenholtz (2019) observed systematic bowl-shaped deformation, substantially lower precision, and larger offsets from reference data (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Above ~120°, the geometric benefit plateaus while image correspondence degrades due to extreme foreshortening and appearance distortion, causing a net increase in reconstruction error (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000022).

### 2. Nadir + Oblique vs. All-Oblique Camera Networks

Fraser's (1984) seminal simulations of a 27-point target array compared six four-camera imaging configurations under identical conditions (image scale 1:40, σ_image = 2.3 μm, inner-constraints datum). The results are summarized below:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Key findings from this comparison include:

- **Convergent θ = 120°** produced the most isotropic precision, with σ_XY = σ_Z = 0.07 mm and very small precision ranges (Δσ_XY = 0.01 mm, Δσ_Z = 0.03 mm), making it Fraser's recommended design for most 3D measurement tasks (pqac-00000028).
- **Convergent θ = 180°** gave the most homogeneous distribution (Δσ_Z = 0.01 mm), though σ_XY was slightly larger than σ_Z (pqac-00000028).
- **Normal + convergent** (a mixed geometry analogous to the user's proposed nadir-plus-oblique layout) performed nearly as well as the all-convergent networks (q = 0.6, σ_Z reduced to 0.09 mm), demonstrating that adding even two convergent views to a nadir-like configuration substantially improves Z-precision (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028).
- **Pure "normal" (near-parallel axis) networks** showed the largest Z-error and the poorest homogeneity, with σ_Z roughly 1.5–2.5× larger than σ_XY (pqac-00000027).

In UAV photogrammetry, Nesbit and Hugenholtz (2019) confirmed that supplementing nadir images with oblique images at **20–35°** tilt improved accuracy and precision by nearly **50%** relative to nadir-only blocks (pqac-00000018). Combination datasets consistently reduced systematic dome deformation, generated more tie points, and produced lower standard deviations than either nadir-only or single-oblique datasets (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015). The precision-to-viewing-distance ratio improved from approximately 1:1000 for nadir-only to about 1:1500 for combination datasets (pqac-00000015).

**Implication for the proposed setup.** A one-overhead plus two-oblique arrangement is a variant of the "normal + convergent" geometry that Fraser showed performs well (q = 0.6). However, the overhead camera provides good XY but poor Z resolution for table-plane-parallel targets. The two oblique cameras provide the convergent rays needed for Z. For near-isotropic 3D accuracy, the three-camera all-oblique alternative (cameras at ~30–45° elevation, spread ~120° in azimuth) would produce more uniform error ellipsoids, consistent with Fraser's finding that the convergent θ = 120° network was the best general-purpose design (pqac-00000028).

### 3. Depth Error as a Function of Baseline, Distance, and Pixel Resolution

The fundamental relationship for stereo triangulation depth uncertainty is well established across the literature. For a rectified stereo pair with baseline B, focal length f (in pixels f_px = f_phys/p, where p is pixel pitch), and target at depth Z, depth is given by Z = f_px · B / d, where d is disparity in pixels. Propagating a disparity measurement error σ_d (typically ~0.5–1.0 pixels for sub-pixel matching) yields:

**σ_Z ≈ Z² · σ_d / (f_px · B)**

Equivalently, in terms of the physical focal length f_phys and pixel pitch p:

**σ_Z ≈ Z² · p · σ_d / (f_phys · B)**

This relationship was derived and confirmed by multiple sources (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010). The key dependencies are:
- Depth error grows **quadratically** with camera-to-target distance Z.
- Depth error decreases **linearly** with baseline B.
- Depth error decreases **linearly** with focal length in pixels f_px (equivalently, with physical focal length f_phys for fixed pixel pitch).
- Larger pixels (larger p) increase depth error for a given physical focal length (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

(2021) confirmed these relationships through a geometric pixel-quantization cone model, showing that increasing baseline or focal length narrows the uncertainty volume, while increasing pixel size or target distance enlarges it (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Llorca et al. (2010) additionally noted that larger baseline and focal length increase the disparity search space and the near-field blind zone, creating design tradeoffs in practical systems (pqac-00000005).

**Numerical example for the proposed setup.** With the Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide (f ≈ 2.75 mm, sensor 6.45 × 3.63 mm, 4608 × 2592 pixels → pixel pitch p ≈ 1.4 μm, f_px ≈ 1964 pixels), a baseline of ~1.0 m, and a maximum gripper distance of ~1.5 m from the closer cameras: σ_Z ≈ (1.5)² × 1 / (1964 × 1.0) ≈ 1.1 mm per pixel of disparity error. Self-occlusion by the robot arm's own links is the primary driver for requiring multiple cameras at different viewpoints. The literature on multi-camera motion capture provides quantitative guidance:

**Angular baseline.** Starck et al. (2009), in their comprehensive study of multi-camera 3D production studios, found that an angular baseline of approximately **25°** between neighboring camera views was optimal for stereo matching, balancing correspondence reliability against depth ambiguity. However, achieving reconstruction error below 50 mm in their experiments required at least 42 cameras (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). These numbers apply to complete surface reconstruction of a complex human body and represent an upper bound for the simpler problem of tracking discrete gripper fingertip markers.

**Non-planar arrangement is critical.** Cameras should not all be placed in a single plane, as this creates systematic blind spots (pqac-00000033). Including cameras at different elevations—including overhead views—reduces phantom volumes from self-occlusion, particularly for an articulated arm that can fold back on itself (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

3. **Consider a fourth camera.** Fraser showed that going from 3 to 4 cameras improves precision by ~20% under the √m rule (pqac-00000029). More importantly, a fourth camera provides critical redundancy when one view is occluded by the arm.

4. **Elevate all cameras to ~30–45°.** An all-oblique arrangement with three cameras at 30–45° elevation and 120° azimuth spacing would approach Fraser's θ = 120° convergent network, which gave the most isotropic and homogeneous precision (pqac-00000028). This configuration also provides better workspace-clearance views than a single nadir camera."}

Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. What do the close-range photogrammetry and multi-view computer vision literatures say about: (1) the optimal intersection (convergence) angle between camera rays for minimizing 3D triangulation error, and how fast the error grows when the angle falls below about 30-60 deg or rises above about 120 deg; (2) whether one near-vertical (nadir) camera plus two low oblique side cameras is a strong network for 3D point accuracy, compared with, for example, three cameras all elevated 30-45 deg and spread about 120 deg apart in azimuth; (3) how baseline, camera-to-target distance and pixel resolution set the depth error; and (4) how self-occlusion by the arm should change the number and spread of cameras (e.g. optimal camera placement for motion capture with occlusion). Give quantitative rules of thumb with citations.

Raising its tilt or elevation would improve the ray-intersection geometry toward the 60–90° optimal range (di2016geopositioningprecisionanalysis pages 4-5, fraser1984networkdesignconsiderations pages 6-7).

2. **Spread cameras in azimuth.** The literature strongly favors cameras distributed ~120° apart in azimuth rather than clustered on one side, to produce isotropic XY precision and maintain visibility during arm self-occlusion (fraser1984networkdesignconsiderations pages 6-7, starck2009themultiplecamera3d pages 26-30).

3. **Consider a fourth camera.** Fraser showed that going from 3 to 4 cameras improves precision by ~20% under the √m rule (fraser1984networkdesignconsiderations pages 7-9). More importantly, a fourth camera provides critical redundancy when one view is occluded by the arm.

4. **Elevate all cameras to ~30–45°.** An all-oblique arrangement with three cameras at 30–45° elevation and 120° azimuth spacing would approach Fraser's θ = 120° convergent network, which gave the most isotropic and homogeneous precision (fraser1984networkdesignconsiderations pages 6-7). This configuration also provides better workspace-clearance views than a single nadir camera.

## Camera Placement for Triangulating a Tabletop Robot Arm: Quantitative Guidance from Photogrammetry and Multi-View Vision

### 1. Optimal Convergence (Intersection) Angle for 3D Triangulation

The convergence angle θ—the angle between two camera rays at the target point—is the single most important geometric parameter for triangulation accuracy. Classical photogrammetric analysis and empirical studies converge on an optimum near **90°**, with a broad practical sweet spot of roughly **60–120°**.

**Geometric basis.** In the stereo depth relation, the depth component of the reconstructed point depends on the reciprocal of the sine of the half-convergence angle. Weinshall (1990) showed that reconstructed depth is proportional to a disparity term divided by 2 sin(α), where the total convergence angle is 2α, establishing an explicit reciprocal-sine dependence (pqac-00000051). This means that at very small intersection angles, depth uncertainty diverges approximately as 1/sin(θ/2), while at 90° the geometric contribution to depth error is minimized.

**Empirical confirmation.** Di et al. (2016), analyzing multi-image triangulation of lunar images, found that overall positional error reached its minimum near a convergence angle of approximately **60°**, while height (depth) error reached its minimum near **90°** (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000046). When image-matching errors were included, the optimal turning points shifted toward somewhat smaller angles because larger convergence angles degrade image correlation and matching precision (pqac-00000046). Li et al. (2014), studying rover localization with the ExoMars PanCam, found optimal convergence angles of **99–100°** for 6-landmark configurations, **100–108°** for 9–12 landmarks, and a recommended operational band of **70–90°** (pqac-00000042). Olague and Mohr (2002) found an optimal convergence angle around **45°** in their multi-camera setup, corresponding to an approximately 90° inter-camera separation, with their image-error model showing that target-localization uncertainty rises sharply as the incidence angle approaches 80° due to foreshortening (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022).

**Error growth outside the sweet spot.** At angles below ~30°, rays become nearly parallel, the system is poorly conditioned, and depth error increases rapidly—approximately inversely with the sine of the convergence angle (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000052). At very small angles (5–15°), Nesbit and Hugenholtz (2019) observed systematic bowl-shaped deformation, substantially lower precision, and larger offsets from reference data (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Above ~120°, the geometric benefit plateaus while image correspondence degrades due to extreme foreshortening and appearance distortion, causing a net increase in reconstruction error (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000022).

### 2. Nadir + Oblique vs. All-Oblique Camera Networks

Fraser's (1984) seminal simulations of a 27-point target array compared six four-camera imaging configurations under identical conditions (image scale 1:40, σ_image = 2.3 μm, inner-constraints datum). The results are summarized below:

| Configuration | Convergence angle θ | q-factor | Mean σ_c (mm) | σ_XY (mm) | σ_Z (mm) | Δσ_XY (mm) | Δσ_Z (mm) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| “Normal,” stations 9–12 | — | 0.7 | 0.09 | 0.07 | 0.12 | 0.03 | 0.09 |
| “Normal,” stations 5–8 | — | 1.0 | 0.12 | 0.08 | 0.17 | 0.03 | 0.12 |
| “Normal” + convergent, stations 2, 4, 5, 7 | 120° for convergent component | 0.6 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.09 | 0.01 | 0.05 |
| Convergent | 60° | 0.8 | 0.09 | 0.07 | 0.13 | 0.02 | 0.09 |
| Convergent | 120° | 0.6 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.01 | 0.03 |
| Convergent | 180° | 0.6 | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.06 | 0.01 | 0.01 |
| **Common simulation conditions** (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028) | **Inner-constraints datum** | **Image scale 1:40** | **σ_image = 2.3 μm** | — | — | — | — |


*Table: Fraser’s 1984 four-image simulations compare normal, mixed, and convergent networks under common scale, image-precision, and datum assumptions. The 120° convergent network gives isotropic XY/Z precision, while 180° gives the most homogeneous coordinate precision.*

Key findings from this comparison include:

- **Convergent θ = 120°** produced the most isotropic precision, with σ_XY = σ_Z = 0.07 mm and very small precision ranges (Δσ_XY = 0.01 mm, Δσ_Z = 0.03 mm), making it Fraser's recommended design for most 3D measurement tasks (pqac-00000028).
- **Convergent θ = 180°** gave the most homogeneous distribution (Δσ_Z = 0.01 mm), though σ_XY was slightly larger than σ_Z (pqac-00000028).
- **Normal + convergent** (a mixed geometry analogous to the user's proposed nadir-plus-oblique layout) performed nearly as well as the all-convergent networks (q = 0.6, σ_Z reduced to 0.09 mm), demonstrating that adding even two convergent views to a nadir-like configuration substantially improves Z-precision (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028).
- **Pure "normal" (near-parallel axis) networks** showed the largest Z-error and the poorest homogeneity, with σ_Z roughly 1.5–2.5× larger than σ_XY (pqac-00000027).

In UAV photogrammetry, Nesbit and Hugenholtz (2019) confirmed that supplementing nadir images with oblique images at **20–35°** tilt improved accuracy and precision by nearly **50%** relative to nadir-only blocks (pqac-00000018). Combination datasets consistently reduced systematic dome deformation, generated more tie points, and produced lower standard deviations than either nadir-only or single-oblique datasets (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015). The precision-to-viewing-distance ratio improved from approximately 1:1000 for nadir-only to about 1:1500 for combination datasets (pqac-00000015).

**Implication for the proposed setup.** A one-overhead plus two-oblique arrangement is a variant of the "normal + convergent" geometry that Fraser showed performs well (q = 0.6). However, the overhead camera provides good XY but poor Z resolution for table-plane-parallel targets. The two oblique cameras provide the convergent rays needed for Z. For near-isotropic 3D accuracy, the three-camera all-oblique alternative (cameras at ~30–45° elevation, spread ~120° in azimuth) would produce more uniform error ellipsoids, consistent with Fraser's finding that the convergent θ = 120° network was the best general-purpose design (pqac-00000028).

### 3. Depth Error as a Function of Baseline, Distance, and Pixel Resolution

The fundamental relationship for stereo triangulation depth uncertainty is well established across the literature. For a rectified stereo pair with baseline B, focal length f (in pixels f_px = f_phys/p, where p is pixel pitch), and target at depth Z, depth is given by Z = f_px · B / d, where d is disparity in pixels. Propagating a disparity measurement error σ_d (typically ~0.5–1.0 pixels for sub-pixel matching) yields:

**σ_Z ≈ Z² · σ_d / (f_px · B)**

Equivalently, in terms of the physical focal length f_phys and pixel pitch p:

**σ_Z ≈ Z² · p · σ_d / (f_phys · B)**

This relationship was derived and confirmed by multiple sources (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000010). The key dependencies are:
- Depth error grows **quadratically** with camera-to-target distance Z.
- Depth error decreases **linearly** with baseline B.
- Depth error decreases **linearly** with focal length in pixels f_px (equivalently, with physical focal length f_phys for fixed pixel pitch).
- Larger pixels (larger p) increase depth error for a given physical focal length (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

Lin et al. (2021) confirmed these relationships through a geometric pixel-quantization cone model, showing that increasing baseline or focal length narrows the uncertainty volume, while increasing pixel size or target distance enlarges it (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Llorca et al. (2010) additionally noted that larger baseline and focal length increase the disparity search space and the near-field blind zone, creating design tradeoffs in practical systems (pqac-00000005).

**Numerical example for the proposed setup.** With the Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide (f ≈ 2.75 mm, sensor 6.45 × 3.63 mm, 4608 × 2592 pixels → pixel pitch p ≈ 1.4 μm, f_px ≈ 1964 pixels), a baseline of ~1.0 m, and a maximum gripper distance of ~1.5 m from the closer cameras: σ_Z ≈ (1.5)² × 1 / (1964 × 1.0) ≈ 1.1 mm per pixel of disparity error. With sub-pixel matching (σ_d ≈ 0.3 px), this yields σ_Z ≈ 0.3 mm, which is within the few-mm drift detection requirement.

### 4. Self-Occlusion by the Arm and Camera Count/Spread

Self-occlusion by the robot arm's own links is the primary driver for requiring multiple cameras at different viewpoints. The literature on multi-camera motion capture provides quantitative guidance:

**Angular baseline.** Starck et al. (2009), in their comprehensive study of multi-camera 3D production studios, found that an angular baseline of approximately **25°** between neighboring camera views was optimal for stereo matching, balancing correspondence reliability against depth ambiguity. In a planar ring, this corresponds to roughly 14 cameras for 360° coverage (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038).

**Minimum cameras for stable coverage.** For full-body surface reconstruction, angular-coverage stability was reached at approximately **16 cameras**, after which additional cameras produced diminishing returns in visibility improvement. However, achieving reconstruction error below 50 mm in their experiments required at least 42 cameras (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). These numbers apply to complete surface reconstruction of a complex human body and represent an upper bound for the simpler problem of tracking discrete gripper fingertip markers.

**Non-planar arrangement is critical.** Cameras should not all be placed in a single plane, as this creates systematic blind spots (pqac-00000033). Including cameras at different elevations—including overhead views—reduces phantom volumes from self-occlusion, particularly for an articulated arm that can fold back on itself (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

**Active viewpoint selection.** Kiciroglu et al. (2020) demonstrated that optimizing camera viewpoints based on predicted pose uncertainty can substantially improve 3D pose estimation accuracy, suggesting that cameras should be positioned where they provide the most information given expected arm configurations, rather than in a generic symmetric arrangement (pqac-00000039).

**Practical guidance for a tabletop arm.** For the specific task of triangulating discrete fingertip features (not full surface reconstruction), the occlusion problem is substantially simpler than full-body capture. Fraser (1984) recommended a minimum of **three intersecting rays** (not in the same epipolar plane) at every target point (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). With the arm's ~0.63 m reach on a 1.29 × 1.36 m table, the arm subtends a relatively small solid angle, meaning three well-placed cameras with the wide 102° × 67° field of view should maintain at least two-camera visibility of the fingertips throughout most of the workspace. A fourth camera would provide redundancy for configurations where one camera's view is blocked by the arm's body or by the gripper approaching the camera.

Luhmann (2010) reported that multi-camera photogrammetric probing systems using 2–4 digital video cameras achieve typical accuracy of 0.1 mm over distances of 2–5 m, with the imaging rays intersecting at large convergence angles to yield homogeneous accuracy in X, Y, and Z (pqac-00000032). This supports the feasibility of achieving sub-millimeter accuracy with a small number of strategically placed cameras.

### Summary of Key Quantitative Rules of Thumb

| Topic | Rule of Thumb / Formula | Quantitative Value | Key Source |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Preferred ray-intersection angle | For isolated-point triangulation with comparable angular noise, aim near a right-angle intersection; **60–120°** is a useful practical band. Angle definitions vary across papers, so compare the actual angle between rays at the target. | Ideal ≈ **90°**; practical ≈ **60–120°** | Simulations found minimum height error near 90° and minimum overall position error near 60°; strongly convergent networks produced homogeneous 3D precision. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028) |
| Rectified-stereo depth uncertainty | `Z = f_px B / d`, hence `σ_Z ≈ Z² σ_d / (f_px B)`. Equivalently, `σ_Z ≈ Z² p σ_d / (f_phys B)`, where `p` is pixel pitch and `σ_d` is in pixels. | Error grows as **distance²** and falls linearly with **baseline** and **focal length in pixels**. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005) |
| Fraser network comparison | Symmetric convergent imaging makes coordinate precision more isotropic than normal or near-parallel imaging; mixed normal-plus-convergent geometry is also strong. | Mean accuracy factor `q`: **0.6** at 120° convergence versus **0.7–1.0** for the two normal networks; 120° gave `σ_XY = σ_Z = 0.07 mm` in the simulation. | (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028) |
| Moderate oblique imagery | Supplementing nadir coverage with oblique images increases parallax, reduces systematic deformation, and fills visibility gaps. | Oblique tilt **20–35° from nadir**; nearly **50%** improvement in accuracy and precision over nadir-only blocks in the studied high-relief scene. | (pqac-00000018) |
| Occlusion-resistant dense capture | For full-body surface reconstruction, distribute cameras non-coplanarly around the subject; neighboring views should retain enough appearance similarity for matching. These counts are not a minimum for fingertip triangulation. | Neighboring angular baseline ≈ **25°**; visibility coverage stabilized near **16 cameras** in the reported studio experiment. | (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036) |
| Li et al. convergence optimum | Error minima occurred over a range rather than at one universal angle; well-distributed tie points changed the optimum. | With 6 landmarks, optimum ≈ **99–100°**; with 9–12, approximately **100–108°** in two tested camera systems; operational band cited as **70–90°**. | (pqac-00000042) |
| Benefit of additional cameras | Once geometry is strong, precision improves approximately with the square root of observation count: `σ_XYZ ∝ 1 / √m`. Geometry matters more than merely adding similar views. | Moving from **2 to 3** cameras gives a substantial gain; **3 to 4** yields about **20%** lower standard error under the approximation. | (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029) |
| Excessively wide view differences | Larger intersection angles improve geometry only until correspondence and target-localization errors rise from foreshortening and appearance distortion. Thus, the geometric 90° preference is not an instruction to maximize angle indefinitely. | Di et al.: height-error curve minimum near **90°**, then increases; Olague–Mohr’s target-localization model rose sharply as incidence approached **80°**. | (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000046) |


*Table: Key geometric and empirical rules for designing a multi-camera triangulation network, including convergence angle, depth uncertainty, oblique coverage, camera count, and occlusion tradeoffs.*

### Recommendations for the Proposed Setup

Based on the literature, the proposed three-camera arrangement (one overhead at 1.2 m, one front-oblique at ~0.42 m height tilted 19° down, one low side camera) provides a reasonable "normal + convergent" geometry. However, several improvements are suggested:

1. **Increase convergence angles.** The front camera at 19° tilt produces a very shallow convergence angle with the overhead camera (~71° from vertical vs. 0° overhead = only ~19° convergence). Raising its tilt or elevation would improve the ray-intersection geometry toward the 60–90° optimal range (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028).

2. **Spread cameras in azimuth.** The literature strongly favors cameras distributed ~120° apart in azimuth rather than clustered on one side, to produce isotropic XY precision and maintain visibility during arm self-occlusion (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033).

3. **Consider a fourth camera.** Fraser showed that going from 3 to 4 cameras improves precision by ~20% under the √m rule (pqac-00000029). More importantly, a fourth camera provides critical redundancy when one view is occluded by the arm.

4. **Elevate all cameras to ~30–45°.** An all-oblique arrangement with three cameras at 30–45° elevation and 120° azimuth spacing would approach Fraser's θ = 120° convergent network, which gave the most isotropic and homogeneous precision (pqac-00000028). contexts.context: For rectified stereo, depth is obtained from the stereo relation z = bf/d, where z is camera-to-target distance (depth), b is the baseline between cameras, f is focal length, and d is disparity. Propagating a disparity error εd gives the approximate depth error εz ≈ (z²/(bf)) εd, with sign depending on the error convention. Thus, depth error grows quadratically with camera-to-target distance and disparity uncertainty, and decreases linearly as baseline or focal length increases. The excerpt expresses this as εz ≈ z² · εd/(bf). Pixel size determines how image-coordinate uncertainty is converted into physical disparity uncertainty. If εd is measured in pixels and pixel pitch is p, then the physical disparity error is εd,pixel p, so εz ≈ z² p εd,pixel/(b fphysical). Equivalently, using focal length in pixel units fpx = fphysical/p, the formula is εz ≈ z² εd,pixel/(b fpx). Therefore, larger pixels increase error for a fixed physical focal length and pixel-level matching error, while focal length expressed in pixels already incorporates pixel size. The excerpt’s simulation assumes one-pixel image noise and an approximately 8 cm ground sampling distance.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that stereo depth is obtained by triangulation from image correspondence and that quantization of disparity limits accuracy. Baseline, focal length, pixel size, and camera-to-target distance determine the resulting range error. For a rectified stereo pair, depth is Z = fB/d, where Z is target distance, f is focal length, B is baseline, and d is disparity. Propagating a disparity error Δd gives ΔZ ≈ (Z²/(fB))Δd. Thus, depth error increases quadratically with camera-to-target distance, decreases with larger baseline, and decreases with longer focal length. Pixel size affects the error through disparity quantization: if the disparity uncertainty is one physical pixel of width p, then Δd in metric image coordinates is approximately p, giving ΔZ ≈ Z²p/(fB). Equivalently, when focal length is expressed in pixels (f_px = f/p) and disparity uncertainty is measured in pixels, ΔZ ≈ Z²Δd_px/(f_pxB). The article emphasizes that selecting baseline and focal length requires balancing depth accuracy against computational cost and the vehicle’s frontal blind zone. The supplied pages describe these dependencies but do not include the paper’s detailed derivation or exact convention for the quantization interval.

It formulates 3D reconstruction as a function of the four measured image coordinates T = (u_l, v_l, u_r, v_r), then propagates pixel-coordinate uncertainty through the Jacobian ∂P/∂T. contexts.context: For an ideal parallel stereo pair, depth is determined by the baseline, focal length in pixels, and disparity: Z = f_x t_x / d_u, where t_x is the baseline, f_x = f/d_x is the focal length measured in pixels, f is the physical focal length, d_x is the physical pixel size, and d_u is disparity in pixels. Thus, for a fixed disparity uncertainty of approximately one pixel, the exact depth change between adjacent disparity values is ΔZ = f_x t_x[1/(d_u−1) − 1/d_u] = f_x t_x/[d_u(d_u−1)]. Since d_u = f_x t_x/Z, the approximate error at target distance Z is ΔZ ≈ Z²/(f_x t_x) = Z²d_x/(f t_x). Therefore, depth error increases approximately quadratically with camera-to-target distance and decreases with larger baseline, longer focal length, or smaller physical pixel size (equivalently, greater image sampling/focal length in pixels). The excerpt also notes that larger image dimensions reduce depth error by increasing the available disparity range, but larger baseline and focal length increase the disparity-search space and frontal blind zone, creating design tradeoffs.

contexts.context: The excerpt models depth uncertainty by representing each quantized image pixel as a finite region extending by half the pixel dimensions, du and dv, around the measured image coordinate. Each pixel region generates a projection cone from its camera center, and the intersection of the left and right cones defines the uncertain 3-D region of the reconstructed object point. The stereo baseline is represented by d: the left camera translation is (0,0,0), while the right camera translation is (0,0,d). The image projections depend on focal lengths f₁ and f₂ and object depth through the perspective relations uₗ=f₁xw/zw, uᵣ=f₂(xw−d)/zw, with analogous y-coordinate equations. Thus, larger baseline generally changes disparity more strongly with depth and reduces triangulation depth uncertainty; larger focal length likewise increases disparity sensitivity and reduces error. Greater camera-to-target distance increases depth error because the same pixel or disparity uncertainty corresponds to a larger range uncertainty. Pixel size determines du and dv, so larger pixels produce wider projection cones and greater depth uncertainty. The excerpt develops this geometrically through intersections of cone boundary lines; the supplied pages do not show the final compact depth-error formula.

contexts.context: The excerpt analyzes stereo-triangulation uncertainty through the volume of the pixel-quantization uncertainty region rather than providing a closed-form scalar formula for depth error. Its simulations find that increasing baseline length decreases error volume: with a fixed target position, the image points move farther from the image centers, narrowing the intersecting projection region. Increasing focal length also decreases error volume because the pixel-unit projection cones become narrower; the paper consequently recommends using a camera with a larger focal length when possible. Increasing pixel size increases quantization error volume because each pixel subtends a wider projection cone. Increasing camera-to-target distance (depth) increases measurement error because the projected pixel cones intersect farther from the cameras, producing a larger uncertainty region. Thus, the qualitative dependence is inverse with baseline and focal length, and direct with pixel size and target distance. The supplied pages do not state an explicit formula for depth error as a function of all four parameters. They describe a geometric model in which pixel quantization defines projection cones, calculate the resulting uncertainty-region vertices and volume, and use that volume as the measurement-error measure. The conclusion specifically confirms the equal-focal-length result for points on a plane parallel to the cameras, while noting approximation limitations for unequal focal lengths.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly compare a nadir-plus-oblique configuration with an entirely all-oblique camera network, nor does it establish a definitive optimal azimuth/elevation geometry for multi-camera 3D networks. It does show that adding oblique imagery to nadir blocks substantially improves UAV–SfM network behavior: systematic dome errors are reduced or eliminated, more points are generated, precision improves, and precision-to-viewing-distance ratios increase from approximately 1:1000 for nadir-only blocks to about 1:1500 for combination datasets. For single-angle oblique blocks, very low off-nadir angles (0–15°) produce bowl-shaped deformation and poorer accuracy, while larger angles improve precision and accuracy; the 20–35° range produced results comparable to published benchmarks. In combination datasets, increasing tilt generally improved precision but could reduce accuracy, indicating a tradeoff. Higher oblique angles provide larger parallactic angles, which benefit camera self-calibration. Oblique patterns containing more images, such as BoxIO and double convergent arcs, yielded the highest precision but sometimes the lowest accuracy. The study also reports that differences among oblique patterns and camera angles were generally subtle and did not decisively identify one optimal configuration.
contexts.question: How does a nadir plus oblique camera configuration compare to all-oblique cameras in photogrammetric network accuracy? What elevation and azimuth angles are optimal for multi-camera 3D networks?

contexts.context: The excerpt directly evaluates nadir-plus-oblique combination datasets against nadir-only and single-oblique configurations, but it does not provide a direct comparison with an all-oblique multi-camera network. Adding oblique images to nadir blocks consistently improved the photogrammetric results: combination datasets reduced or eliminated systematic dome deformation, generated more points, produced lower standard deviations (higher precision), and had comparable or better mean differences than nadir-only datasets. The authors state that these improvements persisted regardless of overlap, oblique camera angle, or oblique image pattern. Differences among the various combination patterns and angles were comparatively subtle and did not establish one universally optimal configuration. For pattern-specific trends, double convergent arcs performed better at lower oblique angles of approximately 10–15°, whereas box patterns were slightly more effective at higher angles of approximately 25–35°, especially under the 70/70 overlap condition. Single-oblique datasets at very low angles (0–15°) showed bowl-shaped deformation, poorer precision, and larger offsets; angles of 20–35° improved accuracy and precision. Thus, the excerpt supports moderate-to-high off-nadir angles and mixed nadir-oblique acquisition, while leaving the optimal elevation and azimuth geometry for all-oblique multi-camera 3D networks unresolved.

Combination datasets containing nadir and oblique images had lower M3C2 standard deviations than single-angle datasets, while high-oblique single-angle configurations (25–35° tilt) generally performed better than nadir-only datasets but still worse than the combination configurations. Single flight-line orientations produced incomplete coverage and gaps, whereas combining NS and EW lines reduced gaps and produced complete datasets. contexts.context: The excerpt provides a comparison between nadir-only imagery and a hybrid configuration combining nadir, oblique, and manually acquired façade-oriented images, but it does not evaluate an all-oblique camera configuration. In the reported two-story-building test without GCPs, the hybrid approach produced substantially better network completeness and accuracy: it reconstructed all 35 reference point positions compared with 21 for the nadir model, reduced vertical MAE from 0.355 m to 0.029 m, and reduced 3D RMSE from 0.454 m to 0.046 m. It also enabled evaluation of all 14 measured lengths and all seven selected surfaces, including upper-floor and under-eave regions, whereas the nadir model covered only four length pairs and four surfaces. The discussion attributes nadir limitations to weak or unfavorable viewing geometry, incidence angles, sparse tie points, and weak ray convergence on vertical façades. However, the excerpt gives no direct comparison with all-oblique imagery and reports no optimal elevation or azimuth angles for multi-camera 3D networks. Therefore, it can support the general conclusion that combining nadir and oblique views improves façade reconstruction and vertical accuracy, but it cannot establish whether that configuration is superior to all-oblique acquisition or identify optimal camera angles.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report a direct comparison between nadir-plus-oblique and all-oblique camera configurations, nor does it provide numerical optimal elevation or azimuth angles. It does, however, describe the criteria that the EPOCA evolutionary system uses to evaluate multi-camera photogrammetric networks. Camera placement is parameterized with a viewing-sphere model to represent three-dimensional convergent networks, and the design considers each camera’s convergence angle toward object features as well as relative camera orientations. Visibility, data sufficiency, incidence-angle limits, and robotic-workspace constraints are incorporated into evaluation, with invalid configurations corrected or penalized. Network quality is assessed through error propagation for the resulting 3D measurements, dynamically considering the object regions and the cameras observing them. Thus, the excerpt supports the general principle that accuracy depends on convergent geometry, adequate visibility, acceptable incidence angles, and redundant observations, but the specific configuration comparison and angle recommendations requested in the question would need to be obtained from another section or source.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that adding oblique/convergent photography to a normal (approximately nadir-oriented) configuration substantially improves photogrammetric network accuracy over conventional all-normal imaging. In Table 2, the normal-plus-convergent network has mean coordinate-error figures comparable to the purely convergent networks, and it performs better than the normal networks. However, the most homogeneous object-point accuracy is obtained with an all-convergent, symmetric geometry having a 180° convergence angle. The 120° convergent configuration is also strong, while the 60° case is less favorable; the table reports the 120° and 180° networks with particularly low coordinate and distance-related errors. Thus, for multi-camera 3D work, a symmetric, strongly convergent arrangement—approximately 120°–180° convergence, with 180° identified as the best of the tested designs—is preferred when site constraints permit. The excerpt does not specify separate optimal camera elevation and azimuth angles, so those angles cannot be derived directly from this passage. It does stress that geometry should provide at least three intersecting rays at every point, with the rays not lying in one epipolar plane. Additional photographs are less important than selecting a strong, homogeneous imaging geometry.

contexts.context: The excerpt addresses mathematical treatment of free or rank-deficient close-range photogrammetric networks, not camera geometry or placement. It states that pseudo-inverse solutions provide “minimum mean variance” estimates for parameters and can produce meaningful precision estimates for object-space coordinate combinations. Seven appropriate nonzero constraints remove network singularity, while an optimally selected absolute minimal constraint minimizes parameter standard error. However, minimum parameter variance does not necessarily minimize object-space positional variance; covariance contributions from exterior orientation, coordinates, and additional parameters must be distinguished. It gives no convergence-angle, baseline, resolution, or occlusion rules.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. What do the close-range photogrammetry and multi-view computer vision literatures say about: (1) the optimal intersection (convergence) angle between camera rays for minimizing 3D triangulation error, and how fast the error grows when the angle falls below about 30-60 deg or rises above about 120 deg; (2) whether one near-vertical (nadir) camera plus two low oblique side cameras is a strong network for 3D point accuracy, compared with, for example, three cameras all elevated 30-45 deg and spread about 120 deg apart in azimuth; (3) how baseline, camera-to-target distance and pixel resolution set the depth error; and (4) how self-occlusion by the arm should change the number and spread of cameras (e.g. optimal camera placement for motion capture with occlusion). Give quantitative rules of thumb with citations.

Object-point precision is assessed through the covariance/cofactor matrix \(Q_x\); a free-network/inner-constraints adjustment provides “minimum mean variance.” Datum constraints affect coordinate precision, while shape parameters (distance ratios and space angles) remain datum-invariant. No specific convergence-angle, baseline, resolution, or occlusion rules are given.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. Give quantitative rules of thumb with citations.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports close-range photogrammetry simulations of 27 targets in a 2 m cube using four-camera “normal” and convergent networks. Convergent cameras subtended 120° at the target, while normal geometry had baseline/distance \(B/D=0.8\), 4 m station distance, 100 mm focal length, and 1:40 imaging scale. A network-quality factor \(q\) is a coarse accuracy indicator; “strong” networks of three or more photographs typically have \(0.5<q<1.2\). Convergent configurations produced substantially more homogeneous and generally smaller coordinate errors than normal configurations (table values roughly 0.07–0.15 mm versus up to 0.38 mm).

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on photogrammetric network precision via least-squares adjustment, not camera convergence angles or occlusion. For full-rank design matrix \(A\), the estimate is \(\hat X=N^{-1}A^TPL\), \(N=A^TPA\), with covariance \(\Sigma_{\hat X}=\hat\sigma_0^2N^{-1}\). Mean coordinate error is \(\sigma^2_{\bar X}=u^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{\hat X})\). Precision worsens as the smallest eigenvalue of \(N\) decreases; the text states mean-square error is “seriously inflated when \((N+k^2P_X)^{-1}\) is near singular.” Photogrammetric networks also require seven datum constraints: three position, three orientation, and one scale.

contexts.context: Fraser’s “Network Design Considerations for Non-Topographic Photogrammetry” (1984) frames camera placement as **first-order design**, the “configuration problem,” while measurement precision is **second-order design** and adding points/observations is **third-order densification**. Precision depends on “the geometry of the network” and measurement quality; reliability concerns detecting systematic errors, outliers, and incorrect functional relationships. The paper uses self-calibrating bundle-adjustment simulations and covariance/cofactor analysis, emphasizing that added observations provide minimal benefit once a network is already “strong.” It does not, in this excerpt, specify convergence-angle optima, depth-error formulas, or occlusion-placement rules.

contexts.context: Olague and Mohr, *Pattern Recognition* 35 (2002), model 3D uncertainty by first-order covariance propagation: \(R_P=J_fR_pJ_f^T\). For image errors \(\sigma_p\), cross-ratio analysis gives \(\sigma_k^2=\sigma_p^2\|J_k\|^2\), with \(\|J_k(0,3,2,1)\|^2=80\). contexts.context: The 1984 photogrammetry study compares six four-camera networks: two “normal,” one mixed, and three convergent, with convergence angles of 60°, 120°, and 180°; normal networks used BID (base/image-distance) ratio 0.8. It reports normal imaging has unequal horizontal/vertical precision, while adding convergent stations “reduced significantly” depth error. Among convergent geometries, 120° produced “a near-isotropic form” and “very homogeneous” point accuracy; point-to-point distance errors were essentially distance-independent, making it the “best” solution for many 3D tasks. Larger image scale, longer focal length, target clusters, and repeated exposures enhance precision.

contexts.context: Luhmann’s review states camera calibration depends on accurate interior-orientation modeling (principal distance/point, radial and decentring distortion, affinity/shear) and self-calibrating bundle adjustment in a “multi-station convergent network.” Weak intersection angles or insufficiently orthogonal camera rotations can prevent reliable adjustment. Fixed cameras should be calibrated using a movable calibration body or scale bar; scale bars provide scale throughout the measurement volume. Multi-camera systems are typically 2–4 cameras, with reported accuracy around 0.1 mm over 2–5 m, while single-camera probing is about 0.1 mm only within a defined panel volume.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specify an optimal camera count or placement for tracking an articulated robot arm, nor does it provide a universal number guaranteeing full visibility. It emphasizes that occlusion and unknown surface visibility are fundamental problems in stereo reconstruction, and that multiple widely spaced cameras help infer visibility and integrate appearance. For full-body capture, reported systems use substantially different configurations depending on the task: examples in Table I include 4–8 cameras for real-time silhouette reconstruction, 8–25 cameras for model-free capture, and a 51-camera dome for dynamic human-scene reconstruction. These examples suggest that camera number must be selected according to required coverage, baseline, reconstruction method, and scene complexity rather than a single fixed optimum. Wide camera placement around the subject (approximately 360° coverage where possible) reduces occlusions during motion, while dense short-baseline arrangements can improve view interpolation but may cover only a restricted viewing range. For a moving robot arm, cameras should be distributed around the workspace and at different elevations, with overlapping fields of view so that at least two or more cameras observe each important surface as the arm articulates. The excerpt supports using more cameras for robust all-around visibility, but does not establish an exact minimum.

For silhouette-based reconstruction, increasing the camera count improves shape accuracy; view-angle coverage stabilizes at approximately 16 cameras, after which adding cameras produces relatively little change in reconstruction error. However, achieving reconstruction error below 50 mm in the reported experiment required at least 42 cameras. For stereo reconstruction, camera placement should balance matching reliability against depth ambiguity. The reported optimum for the adopted area-based stereo method is a 25° baseline. In a planar camera-ring arrangement, this corresponds to roughly 14 cameras; the text states that a non-planar configuration requires 14 cameras or more. These values are not a definitive number for full visibility of an articulated body: occlusion depends on the arm’s range of motion, body geometry, and camera placement. The excerpt emphasizes that surface reconstruction ideally needs every surface region visible in multiple camera views, so cameras should be distributed around the subject rather than concentrated on one side. For robust motion capture under self-occlusion, the cited results suggest using a surrounding ring or 3D arrangement, with at least about 14 cameras for stereo geometry, around 16 for stable angular coverage, and substantially more—potentially 42 or more—when high silhouette accuracy is required.
